Respiratory measurements conducted on captive Red-backed mousebirds at body temperatures approximating 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] revealed a maximum basal metabolic rate of 83 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 83 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns closely with predictions for a frugivorous bird of this body size. This relatively elevated oxygen consumption likely reflects the energetic demands of maintaining a high and stable core temperature typical of the Coliiformes, a group known for their pronounced thermoregulatory capabilities. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive individuals resting in darkness during their inactive phase, ensuring that the recorded value represents true basal conditions rather than routine metabolic expenditures. Interestingly, this metabolic rate is somewhat higher than those reported for several sympatric passerines of comparable mass, suggesting that the mousebird's largely folivorous and frugivorous diet may necessitate a more active digestive physiology.

Morphometric data from field-caught individuals indicate that the ultimate wet weight for females averages 61.35 grams [Wwi = 61.35 grams], placing this species among the larger representatives of the genus Colius. This adult body mass is achieved through a distinctive growth trajectory that begins with a remarkably small neonate. Based on measurements from the closely related Colius striatus, the wet weight at birth is estimated at approximately 3.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.2 grams], which represents only about five percent of the eventual female asymptotic mass. Such altricial neonates are entirely dependent on parental provisioning and exhibit rapid initial mass gain during the first week post-hatching.

Incubation under controlled conditions at 39 °C [T = 39 °C] yields an incubation period of 13 days [ab = 13 days] before hatching occurs, a duration that falls within the range of 12 to 14 days reported for the species. This relatively abbreviated incubation is characteristic of many small to medium-sized altricial birds and is thought to reduce the window of vulnerability for the clutch to predation and adverse weather. Following hatching, the nestling period proceeds rapidly, with the young achieving fledging at 11 days after hatching [tx = 11 days after hatching] when maintained at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This developmental pace is noteworthy given the chick's small initial size at hatching.

Reproductive output in females is limited by the constraints of a single annual nesting attempt, with clutches typically containing 1 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 4 eggs per clutch] and a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year]. The onset of breeding is delayed until the individual has completed substantial somatic growth, with the time since birth at first brood recorded at 1.3 years since birth [tR = 1.3 years since birth] under the same standard thermal conditions at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Interestingly, sexual maturation appears to occur earlier than first reproduction, with the time since birth at puberty estimated at 33 days [tp = 33 days], also measured at 40.5 °C. at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]This gap between physiological maturity and actual reproductive activity suggests that social or ecological factors, rather than physical readiness, dictate the timing of the initial breeding attempt.

Longevity records from both wild and captive populations indicate that the maximum lifespan for the Red-backed mousebird reaches approximately 11.5 years [am = approximately 11.5 years] under the favourable thermal regime of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a figure that is exceptional among birds of comparable adult body mass. This extended lifespan aligns with a life-history strategy characterized by low annual fecundity, delayed first reproduction, and prolonged parental investment in a small number of offspring. The species' ability to persist for over a decade likely reflects a combination of low extrinsic mortality rates in its relatively predator-scarce woodland habitats and a robust physiological capacity for somatic maintenance. Such longevity and the associated slow pace of life place Colius castanotus near the slow end of the avian fast-slow continuum.
